context.problemStatement:
Implement the `Lambda` case of `eval`. An anonymous function `fn(x) { ... }`
evaluates to a function value. Nothing in its body is evaluated until it is
called, so this case never returns an error. Build a `VFunc(UserFn(...))` whose
name is `"lambda"` (used in error messages) and whose parent is the environment
in which this function was *defined*, not the one in which it will be called. This
is what lets a function use the names around it, even after the call that created it
has returned.

```
// In eval:
    Lambda(params, body) ->
      // YOUR CODE HERE (replace the code below)
      Error(errors.NotImplemented(
        "Lambda("
        <> string.inspect(params)
        <> ", "
        <> string.inspect(body)
        <> ")",
      ))
```

Run the tests:

```
gleam test -- q8
```

targets.claim: Student can explain why their Lambda case never returns an error even when the body of the anonymous function uses an unbound name, and when such an error would appear instead.

probes.question: In your `Lambda(params, body)` arm, why does evaluating an anonymous function whose `body` contains an unbound variable succeed with `Ok(...)`, and when would that unbound variable error actually be raised?
probes.reason: Directly assesses both parts of the claim: why evaluating the lambda definition itself does not error on unbound names, and at what stage the error is actually triggered.

probes.question: If we pass `Lambda(["x"], Var("unbound"))` into your `eval`, what does your `Lambda` arm return, and what would have to happen for an error about `"unbound"` to be returned?
probes.reason: Provides a concrete expression example to verify the student understands why definition succeeds and when execution/error reporting actually occurs.
